## In one sentence

Randomisation protects comparisons from systematic allocation bias, while
blocking removes predictable variation before treatment effects are estimated.

## Randomisation

Assign units to treatments using a stated random procedure. Simple
randomisation is easy but can create imbalance by chance, especially in small
experiments. Restricted or stratified randomisation can preserve balance while
retaining the protection of chance.

## Blocking

Create blocks from units expected to be similar, then randomise treatments within
each block. A block might be a field, batch, school, or time period. Blocking is
useful when between-block variation is large and treatment can be applied within
blocks.

A block should be based on a pre-treatment characteristic, not a consequence of
the treatment.

::: {.callout-tip}
Do not confuse blocking with matching after the experiment. The allocation rule
and analysis should be decided before outcomes are observed.
:::

## Check your understanding

For a field trial with a north-to-south fertility gradient, propose blocks and a
within-block allocation plan.
